extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, social scientists, and educated readers interested in scientific method and political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and limits of applying scientific (inductive and deductive) methods to the study of individual character and social phenomena; guidance on what methods are appropriate, how to verify theories, and how to derive practical precepts from scientific laws. Emphasizes the special difficulties of social inquiry and the necessary relation between a priori deduction and a posteriori verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest generalizations often earliest ascertained
rubrics_metrics.description: The very highest generalizations were those earliest ascertained with any scientific exactness; e.g., in mechanics, the laws of motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These most general truths may initially lack acknowledged universality until successfully employed to explain many classes of phenomena. The practice of arriving at large general laws early is not intrinsically vicious; what was wrong in ancient practice was making such generalizations without rigorous inductive warrant and applying them deductively without verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification a posteriori must accompany deduction a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification _a posteriori_ must proceed _pari passu_ with deduction _a priori_. The inference given by theory about effects must be tested by specific experience whenever obtainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions of theory cannot be trusted unless confirmed by observation; conclusions of observation are not reliable unless affiliated to theory. Consilience of a priori reasoning and specific experience forms the only sufficient ground for principles in sciences dealing with complex concrete phenomena (e.g., Ethology, social science). Example: Newton’s theory had to be checked by deduction of Kepler’s laws rather than by deducing all observed planetary positions individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of investigation: begin where real induction is feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain first those truths 'in respect to which the conditions of a real induction can be first and most completely realized.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where investigation can reach causes (not stopping at empirical laws of effects), simplest cases—those involving fewest causes—are most amenable to induction and elicit the most comprehensive laws. Thus in sciences of causes it is usual and desirable first to obtain the highest generalizations and then deduce more special ones from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethology should be deductive from Psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethology, the science of formation of character (social/collective character), is a deductive science: 'Ethology, the deductive science, is a system of corollaries from Psychology, the experimental science.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress requires (1) deducing ethological consequences of particular circumstances and comparing with recognized experience; and (2) empirical study of human types by observers capable of analyzing circumstances and explaining characteristics by psychological laws, with any residuals ascribed to congenital predispositions. Eventually transform middle principles into practical precepts adapted to individual circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consilience: agreement of theory and specific experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The accordance of a priori reasoning and specific experience—the consilience of the two kinds of evidence—forms the only sufficient ground for principles of any science 'so immersed in matter' as Ethology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The science must continually verify and correct its deductions by general observations and historical evidence. Both theory and observation are necessary: one without the other is insufficient in complex domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective of social science: causal understanding for guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of society should enable us to understand the causes making a social state what it is; whether it is tending to changes; what effects each feature is likely to produce; and by what means any of those effects might be prevented, modified, or accelerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although precise long-term prediction is impossible because of innumerable and changing circumstances, sufficient laws could allow useful guidance for a given country/time when individual circumstances are well known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Chemical/Experimental method for social phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Chemical' or Experimental mode treats social facts like chemical experiments—seeking specific experience in place of grounding on human nature—which is inappropriate because it ignores that social phenomena are reducible to laws of individual human nature and because controlled experiments are impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include drawing sweeping conclusions from single unanalyzed historical examples or arguing from mere coincidence (e.g., 'England has flourished under prohibitions; therefore prohibitions cause wealth'), and relying on raw historical parallels (Athens, Rome, the French Revolution) without elimination of competing causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference inadequacy in social inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Difference requires finding two instances identical in every respect except the circumstance under inquiry—an experimentum crucis—but such matched instances (e.g., two nations identical save for commercial policy) are impossible in social science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences of legislation reflect deeper differences in position, opinions, habits, institutions, etc., opening an unassignable array of further causes. Hence the most conclusive form of experimental induction is unavailable for political or social questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Method of Difference limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing classes of instances (one with a circumstance, others without) — the Indirect Method of Difference — is inconclusive because prosperity or other social effects are collective results of many favorable circumstances; matching subsets cannot isolate a single causal factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a restrictive nation is richer than several free-trade nations each sharing only part of its circumstances, this does not prove restriction caused prosperity—it may be the aggregate of overlapping favorable conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement fails under plurality of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding numerous prosperous nations that all happen to have restriction in common does not imply restriction caused prosperity when effects admit multiple causes; elimination of other antecedents does not show a single antecedent is causal where many causes may operate jointly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We can at most conclude an effect can sometimes be produced without that antecedent, not that the antecedent never contributes. Social phenomena typically involve innumerable co-operating causes, so Agreement yields minimal presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations insufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Concomitant variations cannot reliably attribute portions of aggregate social attributes to single causes because attributes are influenced by innumerable causes and mutual interactions—variations of the aggregate do not proportionally track any single component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When causes produce effects that are not separable in kind and co-act on the same aggregate, proportional relationships between one cause and the aggregate cannot be established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues is supplementary and presupposes deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Residues (subtract known tendencies to attribute the remainder to other circumstances) presupposes that causes producing part of the effect are already known—knowledge which must come from deduction from principles of human nature rather than from specific experience alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience here supplements deduction: we subtract effects of known causes (deduced from psychological laws) and ascribe the residue to remaining circumstances. Thus experimental argument in politics primarily serves to verify deductive conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social science should not be modeled on Geometry (abstract method) blindly
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Geometrical' or Abstract method inappropriately assimilates social science to geometry, which deals with co-existent facts and lacks conflicts of causes; social sciences involve conflicting and counteracting causes and so are unlike pure geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who adopt a geometrical model err because they neglect the plurality and interaction of causes characteristic of social phenomena. The proper deductive models are the physical sciences of causation (e.g., mechanics, astronomy) where deduction is combined with empirical considerations of conflicting forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of causes: social phenomena derive from individual human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: All phenomena of society are phenomena of human nature, generated by the action of outward circumstances upon masses of human beings; in social phenomena the 'Composition of Causes' is the universal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must reduce social effects to the laws of individual human nature—social beings have no properties except those derived from individual laws. Therefore reasoning grounded on principles of human nature is essential in political or social analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid universal precepts in political art; adapt to circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The phenomena of society may conform to universal laws while practical art (politics) lacks universal rules because results depend on a great variety of circumstances; the art may only recommend watching particular case circumstances and adapting measures accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect one remedy for all social 'diseases'—policy must be adapted case by case according to scientific principles that explain how circumstances produce effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of elaborate selection and comparison of instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound political theory requires careful selection and elaborate comparison of instances; forming theories upon a few casual coincidences or unweighed historical parallels is a gross misconception of method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners who rely on casual examples or parroted Baconian precepts without deeper understanding are liable to error. Proper inquiry demands familiarity with conditions of experimental investigation and, where induction fails, recourse to deductive analysis from human nature.
